A provisional comparison puts Switzerland at 19,773 transport-company records, Japan at 180,319, and the UK at 174,242 in the same worldwide commercial directory. Dividing by country area gives approximately 479 records per 1,000 km² in Switzerland, 477 in Japan, and 715 in the UK. However, these are directory counts—not a verified census of all active, independent transportation companies—and the supplier publishes conflicting totals on its country-specific pages.companydata+2

Counts and geographical density

I have interpreted “transportation companies” broadly: businesses carrying passengers or goods by road, rail, water and air, plus the warehousing and freight-support activities included in the source. This is not a count limited to public-transport operators. The worldwide directory describes its coverage using SIC groups 40, 41, 42, 44 and 45, plus freight-arrangement code 4731.companydata

For consistency, the main comparison below uses all three counts from that directory’s worldwide page, dated 28 October 2026, rather than mixing its different country-page definitions.companydata

What this comparison suggests

On this particular dataset:

  • Japan has about 9.1 times Switzerland’s transport records, but almost exactly the same number per unit of area.

  • The UK has about 8.8 times Switzerland’s records and approximately 49% greater geographical record density.

  • Switzerland and Japan are too close—less than 1% apart on this measure—to justify a meaningful density ranking given the data limitations. These comparisons are calculated from the directory counts and published country areas.bfs.admin+3

Why these cannot be called definitive counts of “all companies”

The important problem is that the source changes its totals and classification scope across pages:

CountryWorldwide-page count, 28 October 2026Country-page count, 21 October 2026Consequence
Switzerland19,77310,019Country-page density falls to 242.7 per 1,000 km²
Japan180,319Not established in this comparisonNo equivalent country-page cross-check
UK174,242146,301Country-page density falls to 600.6 per 1,000 km²

The Swiss country page lists a narrower selection of NACE classes; the UK country page identifies its filter as divisions 49–51. The worldwide page describes a broader SIC-based selection including warehousing and freight arrangement. These are therefore not interchangeable populations, and the differences should not simply be interpreted as one week of business growth.companydata+2

There is also a counting-unit issue: the worldwide directory explicitly includes branch records alongside single-location businesses and head offices. Consequently, its “companies” are not necessarily unique independent enterprises or consolidated corporate groups.companydata

An official UK benchmark illustrates why the definition matters: the Office for National Statistics reported approximately 114,000 VAT- and/or PAYE-registered transport-and-storage businesses, including postal activities, in March 2025. That has a different date, industry scope and registration threshold from the commercial-directory figures.ons

Accordingly, the defensible finding is that the UK has the highest record density in this directory. A definitive Switzerland-versus-Japan ranking is not established.

Which density metric is most useful?

The right metric depends on what you want to understand:

ObjectiveMetric to useWhat it measures
ObjectiveMetric to useWhat it measures
Geographical business concentrationActive transport enterprises per 1,000 km²How concentrated the business population is across national territory
Business supply relative to populationActive transport enterprises per 100,000 residentsNumber of enterprises relative to potential users
Public-transport availabilityService-kilometres per resident, stop coverage and frequencyThe service people can actually access
Industry fragmentationEnterprises alongside employment or revenue per enterpriseWhether activity is spread across many small firms or fewer large ones

For your requested comparison, I would retain companies per 1,000 km², but pair it with companies per 100,000 residents and separate passenger transport from freight/logistics. A company count alone cannot distinguish a small owner-driver business from a national transport operator, so it should not be read as a measure of service quality or transport capacity.

What is—and is not—in the attached data

It is not a complete company-by-company list. The public directory pages show samples and advertise full exports through a database/API or paid file delivery; those underlying records were not retrieved or independently deduplicated here.
